questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java?
questions.title: == vs .equals() in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`==` compares references** (memory addresses) for objects, and values for primitives. **`.equals()`** compares the logical content of objects. For strings: `==` checks if both variables point to the same object; `.equals()` checks if the strings contain the same characters.

interviewer_intent.testing: One of the most fundamental Java gotchas — every Java developer must know this cold
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == to compare Strings or any object and getting unexpected false/true results
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the String pool can make == accidentally work for string literals (both point to pool), which is exactly why it's dangerous to rely on ==

sections.title: Reference Equality vs Content Equality
sections.content:
```java
String a = "hello";          // points to String pool
String b = "hello";          // same pool object
String c = new String("hello"); // new heap object

System.out.println(a == b);         // true (same pool ref)
System.out.println(a == c);         // false (different objects)
System.out.println(a.equals(c));    // true (same content)
```

For **primitives**, `==` compares values directly (no objects involved):
```java
int x = 5, y = 5;
System.out.println(x == y);  // true — comparing values
```

Always use `.equals()` to compare String content. The fact that `a == b` returns true above is an implementation detail of the String pool — never rely on it.

sections.title: == vs .equals()
sections.content:
| Aspect | == | .equals() |
|---|---|---|
| For primitives | Compares values | N/A (primitives have no methods) |
| For objects | Compares memory addresses | Compares logical content |
| For String literals | May return true (pool) | Always correct |
| For new String() | Returns false | Returns true if content matches |
| Null safe | Yes (null == null is true) | No (null.equals() throws NPE) |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: So `==` and `.equals()` do very different things for objects. `==` compares memory addresses — it asks 'are these two variables pointing to the exact same object in memory?' `.equals()` compares the content — 'do these two objects represent the same value?' For strings, this matters a lot. If you compare two string literals with `==`, it might actually return true because Java puts them both in the string pool — the same object. But if you use `new String()`, you get a new heap object and `==` returns false even if the content is identical. So the rule is: always use `.equals()` to compare string content. For primitives, `==` is fine since they're values, not objects.

questions.question: What is the difference between pre-increment (++i) and post-increment (i++) in Java?
questions.title: Pre-increment vs Post-increment in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Pre-increment (`++i`)** increments the value first, then returns the new value. **Post-increment (`i++`)** returns the current value first, then increments. The difference only matters when the expression's value is being used — in standalone statements like `i++` or `++i` on their own line, both behave identically.

interviewer_intent.testing: A classic output-prediction question — tests whether candidates understand evaluation order
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking ++i and i++ always give different results, or getting confused in compound expressions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the classic compound expression example `int b = ++i + i++` and explain step by step

sections.title: Pre vs Post Increment
Key Points
sections.content:
- `++i` (pre): increment first, return new value
- `i++` (post): return current value, increment after
- In standalone statements (`i++;` or `++i;`), they're **identical**
- The difference appears when the expression value is **used** (assigned, printed, passed)
- Both can appear in for loop update section — `i++` is conventional but `++i` works the same
- Pre-increment can be marginally faster for objects (no temp copy needed) — historically important for iterators in C++

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Pre-increment `++i` increments the value and then gives you the new value. Post-increment `i++` gives you the current value and then increments. When you just write `i++` or `++i` as a standalone statement, there's no difference — both increment i by 1. The difference only shows up when you're using the result. So `int a = ++i` — if i was 5, a gets 6. But `int a = i++` — a gets 5, and then i becomes 6. A quick way to remember: the operator's position tells you the order — prefix means increment first, suffix means use first.

questions.question: What is short-circuit evaluation in Java and how do && and || use it?
questions.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation with && and || in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Short-circuit evaluation** means Java stops evaluating a logical expression as soon as the result is determined. For `&&`: if the left side is false, the right side is never evaluated. For `||`: if the left side is true, the right side is never evaluated. This is both a performance feature and a common null-safety technique.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of logical operators beyond just 'and/or' — the evaluation order has practical safety implications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that side effects in the right-hand expression might not execute due to short-circuiting
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the null check pattern `if (obj != null && obj.getName().equals("foo"))` where short-circuit prevents NPE

sections.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation
Key Points
sections.content:
- `&&` (short-circuit AND): stops if left side is **false**
- `||` (short-circuit OR): stops if left side is **true**
- `&` and `|` are bitwise operators that also work as non-short-circuit logical operators — always evaluate both sides
- Short-circuit prevents NullPointerException when checking null before using a reference
- Side effects in the right expression **may not execute** — be careful with methods that modify state
- This is the standard Java null-check pattern: `if (obj != null && obj.doSomething())`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Short-circuit evaluation means Java is smart about stopping early. With `&&`, if the left side is already false, there's no way the whole expression can be true, so Java doesn't even bother running the right side. With `||`, if the left side is already true, the result is definitely true, so the right side is skipped. This has a really practical use in null checks — you write `if (obj != null && obj.getName() != null)`, and if obj is null, Java stops after the first check and never tries to call getName(). If you used single `&` instead of `&&`, it would try to call getName() even on a null reference and throw a NullPointerException.

questions.question: What is the ternary operator in Java and how is it different from if-else?
questions.title: Ternary Operator in Java
questions.direct_answer: The **ternary operator** `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse` is a compact expression that returns one of two values. Unlike `if-else` (a statement), the ternary is an **expression** — it produces a value and can be used inline in assignments, method calls, or string concatenation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Familiarity with compact Java syntax and the expression vs statement distinction
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Nesting ternaries more than one level deep, making code unreadable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that ternary is an expression (produces a value), while if-else is a statement (executes code) — this is why ternary can be used inline

sections.title: Ternary Operator Syntax
Key Points
sections.content:
- Syntax: `condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse`
- Both branches must produce **compatible types**
- It's an **expression**, not a statement — produces a value
- Can be used inline in assignments, `System.out.println()`, or passed to methods
- Avoid deep nesting (more than one level) — prefer if-else for complex logic
- Java compiler can't use ternary for void operations (both branches must return a value)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The ternary operator is a compact way to write a simple if-else when you're choosing between two values. The syntax is `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`. The key difference from if-else is that the ternary is an expression — it produces a value, so you can use it directly in an assignment or pass it to a method. An if-else is a statement that executes blocks of code. So instead of a 5-line if-else just to assign one variable, you can write it in one line. That said, avoid nesting ternaries — it gets unreadable quickly, and at that point you're better off with a clear if-else.

followup_questions: Is the ternary operator a statement or an expression?
When is it better to use if-else instead of the ternary operator?

questions.question: What are bitwise operators in Java and give a practical example of when to use them?
questions.title: Bitwise Operators in Java — Practical Use Cases
questions.direct_answer: **Bitwise operators** operate on individual bits of integer values: `&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR), `~` (NOT), `<<` (left shift), `>>` (right shift). Practical uses include checking if a number is even/odd (`n & 1`), powers of 2 operations, and working with flags/permissions represented as bit masks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of low-level operations and practical programming skills — often appears in algorithm rounds
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing bitwise & with logical &&, or not knowing any practical use case
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the classic interview trick: `n & 1 == 0` to check even/odd without modulo, and `n << 1` for multiply by 2

sections.title: Bitwise Operators Overview
sections.content:
```java
int a = 5;  // binary: 0101
int b = 3;  // binary: 0011

System.out.println(a & b);   // AND:  0001 = 1
System.out.println(a | b);   // OR:   0111 = 7
System.out.println(a ^ b);   // XOR:  0110 = 6
System.out.println(~a);      // NOT: ...11111010 = -6
System.out.println(a << 1);  // Left shift: 1010 = 10 (multiply by 2)
System.out.println(a >> 1);  // Right shift: 0010 = 2 (divide by 2)

// Practical: check even/odd
if ((n & 1) == 0) System.out.println("even");
else System.out.println("odd");
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `n & 1 == 0` → even check (faster than `n % 2 == 0` for many JVMs)
- `n << k` → multiply by 2^k; `n >> k` → divide by 2^k
- `n ^ n == 0` → XOR of a number with itself is 0 (used in 'find unique element' problems)
- `n ^ 0 == n` → XOR with 0 gives the number itself
- `&` and `|` on booleans are **non-short-circuit** versions
- `>>>` is unsigned right shift (fills with 0s), `>>` is signed (fills with sign bit)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of a number. The most practical ones to know for interviews are: `&` for AND — used to check specific bits, like `n & 1` to check if a number is odd or even. `|` for OR — setting specific bits. `^` for XOR — which has the neat property that a number XOR'd with itself is 0, which shows up in problems like 'find the element that appears only once in an array.' Shift operators `<<` and `>>` are multiplying and dividing by powers of 2. These come up occasionally in algorithm problems and are good to mention when you're discussing optimization.

questions.question: What is operator precedence in Java and what is a common pitfall with it?
questions.title: Operator Precedence in Java — Common Pitfalls
questions.direct_answer: **Operator precedence** determines the order in which operators are evaluated in an expression. A classic pitfall is with `+` and string concatenation: `"Result: " + 1 + 2` prints `"Result: 12"` not `"Result: 3"` because `+` is left-to-right and the first `+` triggers string concatenation mode.

interviewer_intent.testing: Attention to evaluation order — the string concatenation precedence trick is a very common interview question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming all operators evaluate left to right equally, or not knowing where parentheses are needed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the string + number gotcha and explain how parentheses fix it: `"Result: " + (1 + 2)` → `"Result: 3"`

sections.title: Precedence and the String Concatenation Gotcha
Key Points
sections.content:
- Multiplication `*` has higher precedence than addition `+`
- Unary operators (`++`, `--`, `!`) have higher precedence than binary operators
- `&&` has higher precedence than `||` — `a || b && c` means `a || (b && c)`
- `+` is left-to-right associative — `"a" + 1 + 2` = `"a1" + 2` = `"a12"`
- When in doubt, use **parentheses** to make intent explicit
- Assignment `=` has very low precedence — everything on the right evaluates first

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The classic Java precedence gotcha is with string concatenation. If you write `"Result: " + 1 + 2`, you get `Result: 12` — not `Result: 3`. Here's why: the `+` operator is evaluated left to right. The first `+` sees a String on the left, so it converts 1 to a string and concatenates: `"Result: 1"`. Then the second `+` sees a String on the left again, concatenates 2: `"Result: 12"`. To get arithmetic addition, you wrap it in parentheses: `"Result: " + (1 + 2)`. This comes up surprisingly often in code reviews, so it's a great one to know.
